newsitem.title: USA: Potential juror says she prays for McVeigh.
newsitem.headline: Potential juror says she prays for McVeigh.

text.p: The courtroom at the Oklahoma City bombing trial went sombre and silent on Friday when a potential juror announced she was praying for defendant Timothy McVeigh, saying she hoped he found inner peace before he was executed.

But she prefaced her remarks by saying, "If he is found guilty." She said if he was, "the sheer magnitude of the destruction leads me to believe the chances of his being executed are pretty good. ... without mitigating circumstances."
McVeigh was accused of planting the bomb that killed 168 people at the Alfred P. Murrah federal building. If convicted, he could be sentenced to death.
The woman, the chief officer of a credit union, was clearly the most articulate and best informed of the 31 people who have been interviewed as the first week of jury selection ended.

The strength of her opinions seemed to startle lawyers and U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch, who have been used to more reticent jury candidates who have difficulty talking about abstract subjects like the death penalty.

McVeigh stared straight at her as she expounded on the seriousness of the bombing and said she hoped that he or whoever is found guilty could find a spiritual guide, like the nun, Sister Helen Prejean, in the film "Dead Man Walking," who could give him "reconciliation and peace" before death.
"To that end I have been praying for Timothy McVeigh for two months," she said, referring to the date she received her notice to report for jury duty.

Like most potential jurors interviewed so far, she said she had either avoided or not noticed the extensive publicity surrounding the case, which the defence claimed interferes with McVeigh's ability to receive a fair trial.

But, unlike almost all of the other jurors, she knew exact details of news accounts that claimed that McVeigh had confessed to his lawyers. She told the court that the defence had claimed one confession did not exist and then admitted it was fabricated.
"I thought it was a slow news day and the media figured they could sell a lot of papers," she said, reflecting the anti-media sentiments of virtually all of the jurors called so far.
She said it would be a hardship for her to serve on the jury because of her credit union duties and no decision was made. But the defence appeared uncomfortable with her death penalty views.
Almost all of the potential jurors questioned this week said they had an open mind about whether the 28-year-old defendant was guilty. Jury candidates were not identified by name.
An Hispanic woman health care company supervisor said first reports about McVeigh's arrest made it look like white supremacist groups were behind the bombing.

But she said she was keeping an open mind because the "media often misquotes or misrepresents things." She said she thought the media took control of the O.J. Simpson murder trial "and the outcome was a result of the media."

McVeigh is formally charged with the "use of a weapon of mass destruction" and the murder of eight federal officials. A second defendant, his former Army buddy Terry Nichols, will be tried separately later. Both pleaded not guilty.
Meanwhile, victims and relatives of those who perished in the bombing sought assurances from Matsch that he would not bar them from testifying even if they listened to the proceedings.

In a request filed with the federal court, the group urged Matsch to "make it clear" that he will not bar the victims from testifying during the penalty phase, when jurors will decide whether McVeigh should be executed or sentenced to life imprisonment.
